name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q01 - Zwitterionic equilibrium of an amino acid

questiontext.text:
The diagram below represents the different ionic forms of an \(\alpha\)-amino acid in aqueous solutions of varying pH:

Identify the zwitterionic form and the pH condition that shifts the equilibrium toward the form carrying a net negative charge.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows three interconvertible ionic forms of an \(\alpha\)-amino acid in equilibrium: Form P (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{N}^+-\mathrm{CH(R)}-\mathrm{COOH}\)), Form Q (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{N}^+-\mathrm{CH(R)}-\mathrm{COO}^-\)), and Form R (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{CH(R)}-\mathrm{COO}^-\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The amino (\(-\mathrm{NH}_2\)) and carboxyl (\(-\mathrm{COOH}\)) groups of an amino acid are ionizable. Protonation of \(-\mathrm{NH}_2\) yields \(-\mathrm{NH}_3^+\) (net \(+1\) charge on that group), while deprotonation of \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) yields \(-\mathrm{COO}^-\) (net \(-1\) charge on that group).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
A zwitterion is a dipolar ion that carries both a positive charge and a negative charge simultaneously, resulting in a net charge of zero. In acidic (low pH, high \(\mathrm{H}^+\)) solutions, protonation dominates; in alkaline (high pH, low \(\mathrm{H}^+\)) solutions, deprotonation dominates.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Inspecting the charges on each species: Form P has only a positive charge (\(+1\)); Form Q has both \(-\mathrm{NH}_3^+\) and \(-\mathrm{COO}^-\) (dipolar, net charge \(0\)); Form R has only a negative charge (\(-1\)). Thus, Form Q is the zwitterionic form.
2. To shift the equilibrium toward Form R (which has a net negative charge), \(\mathrm{H}^+\) must be removed from \(-\mathrm{NH}_3^+\), which occurs in an alkaline (high pH) solution.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Charge balance confirms Form Q is neutral and dipolar, while Form R is anionic and favoured at high pH. Therefore, Form Q is the zwitterionic form, and an alkaline (high pH) solution shifts the equilibrium toward the negatively charged form.

answer.text: Form P is the zwitterionic form; acidic (low pH) solution
Form Q is the zwitterionic form; alkaline (high pH) solution
Form R is the zwitterionic form; neutral pH solution
Form Q is the zwitterionic form; acidic (low pH) solution

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q02 - Potential energy diagram and activation energy with enzyme

questiontext.text:
Observe the potential energy diagram of a biochemical reaction converting Substrate (S) into Product (P):

Which of the following statements accurately interprets the labelled energy levels and curves in the graph?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The graph plots potential energy on the vertical axis against reaction progress on the horizontal axis. Substrate (S) starts at an intermediate potential energy level, rises to a transition state peak, and drops to Product (P) at a lower potential energy level. Two pathways are shown: an upper curve with energy barrier \(E_1\) and a lower curve with energy barrier \(E_2\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Potential energy increases upward along the vertical axis. The energy difference between the average energy content of Substrate (S) and the transition state peak represents the activation energy of the pathway.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
If Product (P) is at a lower potential energy level than Substrate (S), the reaction releases energy and is exothermic. Enzymes accelerate reactions by lowering the activation energy barrier without altering the initial energy of S or the final energy of P.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Comparing S and P: P lies below the dashed baseline of S, so P has lower potential energy than S. Therefore, the reaction is exothermic.
2. Comparing the two barriers: \(E_1\) spans from S to the higher transition state peak (pathway without enzyme), whereas \(E_2\) spans from S to the lower transition state peak (pathway with enzyme). Thus, the enzyme lowers the activation energy from \(E_1\) to \(E_2\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both curves begin at the same energy for S and end at the same lower energy for P, confirming an exothermic reaction in which the enzyme reduces the activation energy from \(E_1\) to \(E_2\).

answer.text: The reaction is endothermic because Product (P) has lower potential energy than Substrate (S), and the enzyme increases the activation energy from \(E_2\) to \(E_1\).
The reaction is exothermic because Product (P) has higher potential energy than Substrate (S), and \(E_1\) represents the activation energy with the enzyme.
The reaction is exothermic because Product (P) is at a lower energy level than Substrate (S), and the enzyme lowers the activation energy from \(E_1\) to \(E_2\).
The reaction is endothermic because Substrate (S) must pass through a high-energy transition state, and the enzyme alters the potential energy of Product (P).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q03 - Effect of substrate concentration on enzyme velocity

questiontext.text:
The graph below illustrates the relationship between substrate concentration \([\mathrm{S}]\) and the velocity of an enzyme-catalysed reaction (\(V\)):

What does \(K_m\) represent on the horizontal axis, and why does the reaction velocity plateau at \(V_{\max}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The graph shows a hyperbolic curve of reaction velocity \(V\) (y-axis) versus substrate concentration \([\mathrm{S}]\) (x-axis). A horizontal asymptote is marked at \(V_{\max}\), and a point on the curve at half-maximal velocity \(\frac{V_{\max}}{2}\) projects vertically down to \(K_m\) on the \([\mathrm{S}]\) axis.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The enzyme concentration is fixed and limited, while the substrate concentration \([\mathrm{S}]\) is progressively increased from zero.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Enzymatic catalysis requires the substrate to bind to the active site of a free enzyme molecule to form the \(\mathrm{ES}\) complex. By definition from the curve, \(K_m\) is the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity equals \(\frac{V_{\max}}{2}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Reading the dashed projection lines: at \(V = \frac{V_{\max}}{2}\) on the vertical axis, the corresponding substrate concentration on the horizontal axis is \(K_m\).
2. Explaining the plateau at \(V_{\max}\): initially, increasing \([\mathrm{S}]\) increases the rate because free enzyme molecules are available. Because enzyme molecules are fewer than substrate molecules, once all enzyme molecules are saturated with substrate, no free enzyme molecules remain to bind additional substrate, so velocity cannot exceed \(V_{\max}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The asymptotic approach to \(V_{\max}\) reflects complete saturation of enzyme active sites, and \(K_m\) marks the substrate concentration giving half-maximal velocity \(\frac{V_{\max}}{2}\).

answer.text: \(K_m\) is the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity reaches \(\frac{V_{\max}}{2}\); the curve plateaus because all enzyme molecules become saturated with substrate.
\(K_m\) is the maximum velocity of the reaction; the curve plateaus because all substrate molecules are completely exhausted.
\(K_m\) is the optimum pH at which velocity is \(\frac{V_{\max}}{2}\); the curve plateaus because the enzyme gets denatured at high \([\mathrm{S}]\).
\(K_m\) is the inhibitor concentration required to halve \(V_{\max}\); the curve plateaus because product inhibition stops catalysis.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BIOMOLECULES_MCQ_Q04 - Secondary structure of B-DNA and base pairing

questiontext.text:
The schematic below represents a portion of the secondary structure of B-DNA:

Which of the following statements about the structure and dimensions of B-DNA is completely accurate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The schematic depicts two polynucleotide strands of B-DNA running in antiparallel directions (\(5' \rightarrow 3'\) and \(3' \rightarrow 5'\)), with sugar-phosphate backbones linked via phosphate groups (\(\mathrm{P}\)), Thymine paired to Adenine with two dashed lines (hydrogen bonds), and Guanine paired to Cytosine with three dashed lines (hydrogen bonds).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In the Watson-Crick model of B-DNA, the sugar-phosphate backbone forms the exterior rails of a right-handed helical staircase, while nitrogenous bases project inward perpendicular to the backbone.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. A phosphate moiety links the \(3'\)-carbon of one sugar to the \(5'\)-carbon of the succeeding sugar through two ester bonds, forming a \(3'\text{–}5'\) phosphodiester bond.
2. For B-DNA, each base-pair step turns by \(36^\circ\), so one full \(360^\circ\) helical turn comprises \(\frac{360^\circ}{36^\circ} = 10\) base pairs.
3. The helical pitch is \(34\text{ \AA}\), giving a rise per base pair of \(\frac{34\text{ \AA}}{10} = 3.4\text{ \AA}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. The strands are antiparallel, not parallel, and are joined by phosphodiester bonds rather than peptide or glycosidic bonds.
2. Adenine pairs with thymine via two hydrogen bonds (not three), and guanine pairs with cytosine via three hydrogen bonds.
3. One full turn of B-DNA spans \(34\text{ \AA}\) and consists of 10 base pairs, with each step turning \(36^\circ\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both the \(3'\text{–}5'\) phosphodiester linkage and the geometric parameters (\(34\text{ \AA}\) pitch, 10 base pairs per turn, \(36^\circ\) turn per step) match the Watson-Crick B-DNA model. Thus, adjacent nucleotides on a strand are linked by \(3'\text{–}5'\) phosphodiester bonds, and one full turn of \(34\text{ \AA}\) pitch comprises 10 base pairs with a \(36^\circ\) turn per step.

answer.text: The two strands run parallel in the \(5' \rightarrow 3'\) direction, and the sugar-phosphate backbone is linked by peptide bonds.
Adenine pairs with thymine via three hydrogen bonds, and one full helical turn of B-DNA contains 12 base pairs with a pitch of \(36\text{ \AA}\).
Each phosphate moiety links the \(2'\)-carbon of one sugar to the \(3'\)-carbon of the next sugar via a glycosidic bond.
Adjacent nucleotides on a strand are linked by \(3'\text{–}5'\) phosphodiester bonds, and one full turn of \(34\text{ \AA}\) pitch comprises 10 base pairs with a \(36^\circ\) turn per step.
